editorial_sections.h2: Where the Peace Symbol Comes From
paragraphs: The peace symbol was designed in 1958 by British artist Gerald Holtom, commissioned for the very first Aldermaston march, a UK anti-nuclear-weapons demonstration organized by the Campaign for Nuclear Disarmament (CND). Rather than inventing an abstract shape, Holtom built it from an existing communication system: semaphore, the flag-signaling code used by sailors.

Semaphore's letter N is signaled with both flags angled downward in a V shape; its letter D is signaled with one flag straight up and one straight down. Holtom overlaid the two letter-shapes, standing for Nuclear Disarmament, inside a circle, producing the three-line design instantly recognizable today. What began as a single-cause protest symbol was quickly adopted by the broader anti-war and countercultural movements of the 1960s, becoming one of the most widely recognized symbols of the 20th century.

faq.a: British artist Gerald Holtom designed it in 1958 for the Campaign for Nuclear Disarmament (CND), for the first Aldermaston anti-nuclear-weapons march in the UK.

faq.q: What does the peace symbol's design actually represent?
faq.a: It combines the semaphore flag-signaling letters N and D, for Nuclear Disarmament, inside a circle. Semaphore N is two flags angled down and out in a V; semaphore D is one flag straight up, one straight down. Overlaid, the two letters form the three-pronged shape inside the circle.

faq.q: How do you type the peace symbol?
faq.a: It falls outside the simple four-digit Windows Alt-code range. Use the Alt+X hex method in Word (type 262E, then press Alt+X), the Character Map, or copy it directly from a reference page. In HTML, use ☮: there's no short named entity.
